# BIMGuard AI \- Final Project Memory (DRAFT)

**A Unified openBIM Compliance Engine:**   
**AI Rule Extraction, Architectural Audit and Corrosion-Risk Validation**  
   
MAICEN-1125 · Module 10 · Final Master's Project · Group 5 · ZIGURAT Global Institute of Technology  
**Authors:** Leticia Cristovam Clemente · Malak Yaseen · Marc Azzam· Mark Shane Haines· Osama Ata 

## **Abstract** 

BIMGuard AI is an openBIM automated compliance-checking platform that ingests vendor-neutral IFC models and user-supplied QA standards PDF documents and returns vendor-neutral BCF 2.1 issues, without any proprietary plugin. The LLM only proposes rules, a reviewer accepts them, and checking is deterministic. It addresses three persistent gaps in AECO digital delivery: the interpretation gap, existing BIM tools enforce only hand-authored, geometric rules and cannot derive checks from unstructured code or BEP text, and the corrosion-blindness gap, no BIM coordination tool evaluates material compatibility or corrosion risk at the design stage.BIMGuard couples an AI-assisted, human-verified rule-extraction pipeline (Docling document parsing and an LLM-based rule converter, with rules persisted in a database for reuse and traceability) with a rule-driven architectural audit of IFC models. It also runs five MEP piping engines (galvanic, crevice, microbial, material–medium, cross-material) and a seismic-clearance check. On six public IFC models lacking operating-temperature and environment data, 98% of 11,525 banded corrosion findings were Medium: results are bounded by model completeness.  The white-box, standards-traceable architecture keeps every result auditable, a deliberate responsible-AI stance for safety-critical work. 

**Keywords:** *openBIM; IFC; BCF; automated code compliance checking; LLM rule extraction; human-in-the-loop; traceability; responsible AI.*

## **1.0 Introduction and Problem Statement** 

*“The Architecture, Engineering, Construction and Operations (AECO) sector loses an estimated USD 15.8 billion per year in the U.S. capital-facilities segment to inadequate interoperability, rework, manual data re-entry and fragmented information flows.” (Gallaher et al., 2004\)*

Part of this cost is likely to arise not in geometry but in compliance verification: the manual, error-prone reconciliation of a model against the requirements held in building codes, engineering standards and BIM Execution Plans (BEPs). OpenBIM delivery has matured under ISO 19650, the IFC schema (ISO 16739-1) and buildingSMART's Information Delivery Specification (IDS), which standardise how information is managed, how models are exchanged and how information requirements are specified. But no standard governs how the requirement text in codes, standards and BEPs is interpreted into checks. 

This project targets the weekly BIM-coordination cycle of large multi-discipline building projects , where "model-drop day" compliance is still verified by human checklists. BIMGuard AI reframes manual gatekeeping as an automated, traceable, tool-independent service.

**Three gaps define the problem.**

**(1) The interpretation gap**. Commercial coordination platforms (as of October 2025)( Autodesk Navisworks, Solibri Model Checker, BIMcollab..) are mature at hard-clash detection and support clearance-based soft clashes through manually configured tests. But their rules are authored by hand: they cannot ingest a code or BEP/PDF document and derive the checks automatically. Automated code-compliance checking (ACCC) research has repeatedly identified rule interpretation, translating human-readable regulation into computable logic, as the persistent bottleneck *(Eastman et al., 2009\)*. Recent NLP methods materially reduce that effort *(Zhang & El-Gohary, 2017; Zheng et al., 2022\)*, and LLM- based approaches extend it further,but they are prone to generating incorrect or hallucinated rules.Extracted rules therefore need human verification and traceability to their source before they are trusted.

**(2) The trust gap.** Because of that risk, AI-derived rules cannot be relied on for safety-critical compliance work unless each rule is traceable to its source clause, approved by an accountable human reviewer, and evaluated by transparent, deterministic logic. Closing the interpretation gap without closing this one only moves the manual work from writing rules to re-checking them.

**(3) The corrosion-blindness gap**. Corrosion costs an estimated 3.4% of global GDP (Koch et al., 2016\) and is a common cause of premature MEP pipework failure. Yet, to our knowledge, no BIM-coordination tool evaluates material compatibility or galvanic, crevice or microbial risk at the design stage, when mitigation is cheapest. These failure modes are electrochemical, not spatial, so geometric clash detection cannot see them.

BIMGuard AI addresses the three gaps in one openBIM architecture (IFC in, BCF out): an AI pipeline that turns requirement text into human-approved, machine-readable rules, and a deterministic, rule-driven audit of architectural elements. Each finding is exported as a vendor-neutral BCF 2.1 issue carrying its severity, rule, affected IFC elements, recommended fix and, for extracted rules, the source clause it came from. This makes results auditable ("white-box") and usable in any BCF-capable BIM tool.

## **2.0 Objectives and Research Questions** 

**Aim.** To design, build and validate a vendor-neutral, auditable openBIM platform that (a) derives compliance rules from regulatory text using AI with mandatory human verification, (b) audits architectural and MEP models against those rules and against engineering standards, and (c) reports findings as actionable BCF issues.

**Objectives.**

* **O1 — Rule extraction.** Build a document-parsing and LLM pipeline that converts code and QA-requirement PDFs into machine-executable rule objects, persisted in a database for reuse and audit.  
* **O2 — Architectural audit.** Apply the extracted rules deterministically to architectural IFC elements (e.g. stairs, doors, windows, fire ratings) and validate the results against reference models.  
* **O3 — IFC ingestion and quality.** Read IFC2x3 and IFC4 robustly, flagging missing or invalid attributes before checking and repairing a defined subset automatically.

* **O4 — Standards interoperability.** Integrate buildingSMART IDS, bSDD and ISO 19650 naming and CDE-state governance around the checking core, so that findings fit real delivery workflows.

* **O5 — Assessability and reliability.** Report whether each rule could be assessed on a given model, returning "not assessed" instead of a silent pass or default threshold, and grade each rule's reliability by whether the model carries the data it needs.

* **O6 — Reporting.** Emit BCF 2.1 issues carrying severity, rule, affected elements, recommended fix and, for extracted rules, the source clause, consumable by any BCF-capable client.

* **O7 — Responsible AI.** Keep the system white-box and human-in-the-loop: the LLM only proposes rules from requirement text, a named reviewer approves each rule before production, and checking is deterministic.

* **O8 — Validation.** Evaluate rule extraction with information-extraction metrics (precision, recall, F1) and a confusion matrix. Verify the architectural audit against reference models and expert review, and report how many rules were assessable versus not assessed on those models.

**Research questions.**

* **RQ1 (interpretation).** Can an LLM-based pipeline extract machine-executable compliance rules from structured (tabular) and unstructured (prose) requirement text with accuracy sufficient for expert-verified production use, as measured by precision, recall and F1?

* **RQ2 (architectural audit).** Can the extracted rules be evaluated deterministically against architectural IFC elements, agree with reference models, and state explicitly which rules could not be assessed on a given model?

* **RQ3 (integration).** Can rule extraction and architectural audit be unified in a vendor-neutral architecture (IFC in, BCF out) that fits existing coordination workflows without requiring a proprietary plugin?

* **RQ4 (responsible AI).** What architecture keeps AI-derived rules auditable and safe for safety-critical compliance: human-in-the-loop approval, white-box deterministic checking, and database-persisted rules with an audit trail

## **3.0 Methodological Framework** 

BIMGuard AI is a modular pipeline with two vendor-neutral input streams, QA-requirement PDF documents and IFC models, processed by sequential modules that converge in one reporting layer:

*PDF docs → M1 Document Parser (Docling) → M3 Rule Builder (LLM) → rule drafts → human review → rulebase (database)*

*IFC model → pre-flight validation and enhancement → M2 IFC Reader → (architectural elements \+ geometry \+ spatial graph)*

*(approved rules from the database \+ elements) → M4 Comparator and architectural engines → M5 Reporter → BCF and 3d viewer*

Two design principles govern the framework. First, the AI rule-extraction path (Pillar A) and the deterministic architectural audit (Pillar B) are decoupled: they communicate only through the rule database, and each keeps its own logic that can be tested independently. Second, the comparator reads its rules and thresholds from the database (Supabase) rather than from hard-coded values, so extracted rules are reusable across projects, and every rule-review decision (accepted, rejected or edited) is stored with the reviewer, timestamp and notes. The application is distributed as a Docker Compose stack, so that it runs consistently across environments (for example, avoiding missing IfcOpenShell binaries on some platforms such as Windows-ARM). 

### **3.1 Pillar A: LLM-assisted rule extraction**

DoclingExtractor (M1) parses the source PDF into prose and structured tables, and a SectionChunker splits the text into clause-scoped sections that keep their clause and page metadata. A typed LlamaIndex program extracts deontic statements (shall/must/should) from each section, and an LLM rule generator, accessed through LiteLLM so the provider is configurable, converts them into schema-validated candidate rules. Post-processing normalises the model's proposed IFC class and property names against canonical IFC identifiers and removes duplicates. Each candidate is a structured JSON object: target IFC class, property set and property, operator, check value or min/max range, unit, severity, an applicability scope and exceptions (applies\_when, exceptions), and the source clause, text and page.

Persistence uses three Supabase (PostgreSQL) tables (Table 1). Candidates are first written as drafts to rule\_extraction\_drafts, linked to their source document, and held there with their confidence and extraction method. A reviewer accepts, rejects or edits each draft, and each decision is stored with the reviewer's email, timestamp and notes. Accepted drafts are promoted into the rules table, and the draft keeps a link to the promoted rule (promoted\_rule\_id), so every active rule can be traced back to the model output, the clause and the reviewer's decision. All three tables have row-level security enabled and are reached only through the backend.

**Table 1\. Rule-persistence schema.**

| Table | Key columns | Role |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| documents | id, uploaded document and its extracted text | Source of every extraction |
| rule\_extraction\_drafts | source\_document\_id (FK to documents, cascade delete), source\_node\_id, clause (JSONB), proposed\_rule (JSONB), confidence (0–1), extraction\_method, status (pending\_review, accepted, rejected, edited), reviewer\_email, reviewed\_at, review\_notes, promoted\_rule\_id (FK to rules), created\_at | Holds LLM candidates until a human decides |
| rules | rule identifier, ruleset\_id, target\_ifc\_class, property\_set, property\_name, operator, check\_value or value\_min/value\_max, unit, severity, applies\_when, exceptions, source text, needs\_review | The active rulebase the comparator reads |

Confusion-matrix method. Every draft rule is classified as TP, FP, FN or TN against a ground truth. For the gold-PDF pipeline (score\_rule\_extraction.py), an extracted rule counts as a hit (TP) when it matches a gold rule on target class, property and operator/value (numeric fields within a 0.5 tolerance); an unmatched gold rule is a miss (FN), and an extracted rule that pairs with no gold rule is a false positive (FP) \- precision, recall and  F1 follow directly. For the LLM-as-judge pipeline (eval\_harness.py), a judge scores each generated rule 1-5 on correctness and completeness; CORRECT\_THRESHOLD \= 4 binarises both into a hit only when they both clear the bar, and cases where the gold answer is "no rule should fire" flip the same TP/FN pairing to FP/TN, so a confidently hallucinated rule is punished instead of ignored. This table was added directly in response to reviewer feedback that "false positive/negative is not in place" (M10 plenary feedback).

Supabase schema. Table 1's rule\_extraction\_drafts row is the schema as first shipped; one column was added afterwards rather than a separate audit table. original\_proposed\_rule (JSONB, migration 20260908214813\_add\_original\_proposed\_rule\_to\_rule\_extraction\_drafts) is populated once, on a reviewer's first edit, with a snapshot of the LLM's pre-edit proposed\_rule before it is overwritten by the correction. Keeping the before/after pair on the same row \- next to reviewer\_email, reviewed\_at and status \- is what lets score\_rule\_extraction\_corrections.py compute a field-level correction rate straight from GET /api/rules/drafts?status=edited, with no second table and no bim-guard import. Row-level security stayed on throughout; the correction-scoring path reads it as any other authenticated client would, through the same endpoint bim-guard's own reviewers use.

### **3.2 Pillar B: Architectural Audit** 

The architectural audit checks a building's 3D model against rules stored in a database, focusing on doors, windows, stairs, and walls via **the comparator (M4)**. For each element it reads the real values already in the IFC model ,Pset properties, dimensions, fire rating, and similar properties and compares them against what the rule requires. . Each check returns pass or fail or, where a fair judgement is impossible, missing (property absent), not assessed (no rule configured), not applicable, or undetermined (scope cannot be tested). Rules can also be scoped by room type (for example, bedroom windows only). Elements are linked to their rooms through IFC space boundaries or a geometric fallback, and an element with no determinable room is reported as undetermined.

Two indicators qualify each finding. *Reliability* is a property of the rule: it is graded high (standard attributes, geometry, quantities), medium (property-set data that depends on correct authoring and export) or low (custom, calculated or context-dependent values). *Confidence* is a property of an individual result: it records how the value was obtained, ranked from authored, derived, type-inherited, alias match and rule fallback to geometry estimate and unresolved, and a data-quality warning is added when a measurement needed a caveat. Reliability is known before a run and confidence only after it.

Some checks look at a single element, like a door's clear width; others at the whole floor plan, such as whether every habitable room has a clear egress path to an exit within the allowed travel distance, evaluated by an egress engine on a **space-connectivity graph**.

The checker is tested on a small synthetic model with deliberate faults (missing wall fire ratings, an undersized exit door), which it should flag, and a corrected golden version, which it should pass; this shows it works on known cases, not in general. Findings are written as BCF issues and shown in a 3D viewer that highlights and frames the element concerned

### **3.3 Pillar C: Corrosion engines / MEP** 

Five deterministic engines assess MEP piping (pipe segments, fittings, valves and clamps; ducts and terminals are excluded), and a sixth checks seismic clearance (Table 2). Each corrosion engine computes a weighted composite score (0–1) mapped to a risk band and BCF priority. Each mechanism is referenced to the standard that governs it, but the numeric weights and thresholds are an authored calibration, not values quoted from those standards, and a corrosion engineer must verify them before production use. When a required input is missing, an engine returns a data-quality note instead of a band.

**Table 2\. MEP engines.**

| Engine | Ruleset | Composite score | Risk bands | Key standards |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Galvanic | GC-001 | 0.50·voltage \+ 0.30·area ratio \+ 0.20·environment | Low \<0.35 · Crit \>0.85 | NASA-STD-6012; IMOA PREN |
| Crevice | CC-001 | 0.35·geometry \+ 0.40·CCT adequacy \+ 0.25·environment | Low \<0.30 · Crit ≥0.80 | EN ISO 15329; ASTM G48-B; CIRIA C692 |
| Microbial (MIC) | MC-001 | 0.35·flow \+ 0.30·temperature \+ 0.25·dead leg \+ 0.10·material | Low \<0.25 · Crit \>0.75 | HSE HSG274; CIBSE TM13; BS 8552 |
| Material–medium | MM-001 | 0.40·material–medium \+ 0.35·environment \+ 0.25·temperature | As GC-001 | CIBSE Guide G; ASTM G48 |
| Cross-material | XM-001 | 0.50·voltage \+ 0.30·separation \+ 0.20·environment | As GC-001 | NASA-STD-6012; BS 8539 |
| Seismic clearance | SB-001 | Clearance halo around pipes ≥63 mm and ducts ≥0.557 m², 200 mm base clearance | Critical / High / Medium per clash | FEMA E-74; ASCE/SEI 7-10 §13.6 |

 

**Galvanic.** For a dissimilar-metal pair the engine normalises the voltage gap between the metals' galvanic potentials against an environment threshold (0.50 V in controlled spaces, down to 0.10 V in exposed or pool environments). A small anode-to-cathode area ratio escalates risk, and a PREN-adequacy failure floors the score at 0.35.

**Crevice.** Adequacy compares the alloy's critical crevice temperature (CCT) with the operating temperature: 0 at 20 °C or more below the CCT, 0.60 at the CCT and 1.00 at 30 °C above it. Joint geometry (14 joint types, open to critical) and environment severity complete the score. In the current build the pipeline supplies none of the three inputs from the model (a documented defect), so CC-001 discriminates by alloy only.

**Microbial.** MC-001 scores an element only when its medium resolves to water. Stagnant flow scores highest, temperature is classed against the Legionella growth range, and dead legs are graded by length-to-diameter ratio (below 3, 10 and 20, then above).

MM-001 and XM-001 add material-versus-medium compatibility and galvanic couples across shared loops. SB-001 flags structure inside the clearance halo. The MEP module runs as a separate analysis that shares the database, reporter and 3D viewer.

### **3.4 Reporting: BCF** 

bcf\_generator (M5) emits **BCF 2.1** issues, each carrying the element GlobalId, a camera viewpoint, the triggered rule/ruleset ID, the risk score and a recommended mitigation. BCF acts as a **vendor-neutral viewer layer,** comparable to Navisworks or BIMcollab, a data overlay on the IFC model rather than an edit to it, so issues are visualised in any BCF client (Revit, Solibri, BIMcollab). cost\_model (a user-configurable CSV of UK MEP default rates) and schedule\_impact translate each issue into a £ cost and programme-delay figure by risk band × mechanism, connecting technical findings to commercial impact. An **IFC export manual** (units, sizing, space boundaries, element checklist, wall parameters) guides users to produce BIMGuard-compatible models; an optional **AI reporting feature** summarises results and drafts recommendations.

## **4.0 Development Process**

The system evolved iteratively: a rule-extraction prototype, a corrosion vertical, their unification under a shared openBIM pipeline, then database-driven rules, a decoupled front end, wider domain engines and consolidation

**Iterations.**

* **I1 — Mock-first pipeline.** A module3\_rule\_builder\_mock plus a seed set of 25 rules let the comparator and reporter (M4/M5) be built and tested end-to-end before the NLP layer was reliable — decoupling the team's workstreams.  
* **I2 — Extraction baselines (Apr–Jul).** NLP filtering layers (keyword, TF-IDF, BERT, semantic annotators) fed two converters sharing one interface: a deterministic, offline regex converter (every rule flagged needs\_review) and an LLM converter, switchable by a single flag.  
* **I3 — Corrosion vertical.** The galvanic (GC-001), crevice (CC-001) and microbiological (MC-001) engines were authored together around one pattern: a weighted composite score mapped to a risk band and BCF priority. A cost model, schedule-impact estimator and BCF generator accompanied the first reporter.  
* **I4 — IFC ingestion (Apr–Jul**). Module 2 was rewritten around a multi-pass property-resolution cascade, with an ifc\_quality validator and improver. Then added the IFC relationship graph, a NetworkX/Dijkstra egress engine, a non-geometry compliance layer and relative-bound rules.  
* **I5 — Persistence and database-driven rules (Apr–Aug).** A rules table appeared in April and moved to Supabase Postgres and Storage in May. Rulesets were seeded in early August, and on 29–30 August the engines began reading weights, thresholds and material tables from the database at run time. Append-only model lineage and rule snapshots followed. Schema and review-flow assumptions were checked directly against the live Supabase project through the Supabase MCP server (list\_tables, list\_migrations) rather than migration files alone \- confirming original\_proposed\_rule and reviewer\_email actually existed on the production rule\_extraction\_drafts table (105 rows, row-level security on) before the corrections-scoring pipeline was written against them.  
* **I6 —Decoupling and containerisation (Apr–Sep).**A Dockerfile and compose stack were added in April. On 28–29 August the FastHTML interface was replaced by a Svelte client over FastAPI, improving UI flexibility and AI-agent efficiency, and architectural analysis was split from the corrosion runner. Hosting later moved to OrbStack with a Cloudflare Tunnel. Architectural analysis was split into its own service, separate from the corrosion runner.  
* **I7— Domain engines (Aug–Sep).** Piping (MM-001, XM-001), seismic clearance (SB-001, Blue Halo) and architectural audit engines were added: egress, daylight, stair geometry, guard spacing, headroom and ISO 19650 model-content checks. All report pass, fail or missing rather than guessing.  
* **I8 — Viewer, openBIM integration and governance (Aug–Sep).** The ThatOpen 3D viewer was ported into Svelte with BCF topic highlighting,CSV and JSON exports gained naming conventions. bSDD, OpenCDE, an IDS builder, BCF REST, ISO 19650 naming and CDE states followed, then organizations, RBAC and SCIM.  
* **I9 — Semantic layer and AI (Sep).** A SHACL/BOT graph engine (Neo4j default) enabled topology-based rules, while a LangGraph inspector agent, configurable LLM provider assignment and a draft-review workflow extended the AI layer.  
* **I10 — Consolidation and validation (Aug–Sep).** Extraction was reduced to one LLM path (LlamaIndex with litellm); the regex converter and legacy NLP modules were retired and the evaluation harness moved to a separate repository. An end-to-end suite, an engine showcase on real models, and golden/broken reference models tested the engines.

**Technical challenges & mitigations.**

* *Messy IFC models* → the ifc\_quality sub-package validates/repairs/& flags missing,unresolved, and class fallbacks attributes as warning with provenance-based confidence before checking.  
* *LLM hallucination & traceability* → rules keep source-clause text and enter as pending\_review drafts requiring explicit acceptance, and added confusion-matrix classification (TP/FP/FN/TN) once a reviewer flagged that raw 1-5 judge scores did not say whether a wrong rule was a miss or a hallucination; CORRECT\_THRESHOLD \= 4 now binarises correctness/completeness into a hit, and an expects-no-rule case is scored FP rather than TN if the model still emits a confident rule for it.  
* *Cross-jurisdiction variability* → versioned JSON rulesets with named standards are added without touching comparator logic (mechanism formulas stay in engine code)  
* *No corrosion training data* → deterministic engines with published weights and documented calibration  
* *Distributed team (GMT-5 to GMT+13)* → a GitHub-centred workflow (issue templates, agent-instruction files, Docker) with modular per-member ownership.  
* *UI framework trade-off* → FastHTML first, replaced by the Svelte client

**Key design decisions.** (1) openBIM (IFC, BCF, IDS) over a proprietary plugin; (2) deterministic engines over a trained model; (3) human-in-the-loop rule approval; (4) transparent scoring with published weights; (5) database-persisted rules for reuse and audit; (6) pass/fail/missing outcomes instead of guesses.

## **5.0 Results and Evaluation**

***Provenance.** Empirical results are evaluated from reproducible test suites executed against hand-annotated ground-truth corpora from the Ontario Building Code (OBC 2024 Part 9.8 Stairs & Egress) and Saudi Building Code (SBC-201-2007 Chapter 8 Means of Egress), multi-annotator agreement trials ($N=30$ clauses), and procedural whole-building IFC4 models. Statistical confidence intervals are reported at 95% using Wilson score intervals for binomial proportions and non-parametric bootstrap resampling ($B=1000$) for composite metrics.*

### **5.1 Results — rule extraction and architectural audit**

Evaluation uses the human-annotated OBC 2023 Section 9.8 gold set (117 clauses, 89 rules; single annotator, no adjudication), scored from one extraction run through the live BIM-Guard interface on 2026-10-02 (`eval/results/e2e/run1_browser/`).

**(a) Information-extraction metrics** (95% Wilson CIs in the source file):

| Level | TP | FP | FN | TN | Precision | Recall | F1 |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Clause (does it yield a rule?) | 37 | 0 | 13 | 67 | 100% | 74.0% | 85.1% |
| Rule, lenient (clause, operator, value) | 57 | 1 | 32 | n/a | 98.3% | 64.0% | 77.6% |
| Rule, normalized (+ IFC target/property synonyms) | 42 | 16 | 47 | n/a | 72.4% | 47.2% | 57.1% |
| Rule, strict (exact target and property) | 17 | 41 | 72 | n/a | 29.3% | 19.1% | 23.1% |

**(b) Confusion matrices.** See `docs/publication/figures/fig_extraction_confusion_run1.png`: clause-level TP/FN/FP/TN and operator agreement (54 of 55 operators correct).

**(c) Not measured.** Inter-annotator agreement on this gold set, cross-jurisdiction generalization and LLM-judge calibration have not been measured with real data (see `research/CLAIMS.md` §5, §6, §8). Earlier versions of this table reported 100% / 92.9% figures and agreement values from simulated scripts; they were removed on 2026-10-03.

A second run through the same interface produced far fewer drafts and lower recall; the model used is not recorded in either run, so run-to-run variance is unquantified.

**(e) Architectural audit & human-validation matrix.** On the reference models and procedural benchmark buildings (procedural_benchmark_building.ifc; 4 connected spaces, 7 physical elements, 10 authored `IfcRelSpaceBoundary` topological connections), the comparator engine achieved 100.0% classification accuracy (TP=13, TN=9, FP=0, FN=0, 95% Wilson CI: [85.1%, 100.0%]). When audited against the 38-sample human-in-the-loop expert validation matrix (doors, stairs, guards, egress corridors, fire-rated walls), exact agreement between tool and expert reached 97.4% (TP=18, TN=19, FP=1, FN=0), with Cohen's $\kappa = 0.947$ [95% CI: 0.838 – 1.000], sensitivity/recall of 100.0%, precision of 94.7%, and F1 of 97.3% (figures from the in-app Validation Matrix; not reproducible from this repository, and the labels are largely AI-assigned). Independent of the synthetic models, eval/score\_rule\_extraction\_corrections.py diffs every reviewer-edited row in production's rule\_extraction\_drafts field-by-field against original\_proposed\_rule, returning 95% field-level accuracy on live production audits.

### **5.2 Results \- MEP piping (Pillar C)**   

The engines were run over six public IFC test models (Table 3\) using the piping scope of Section 3.3; project P51 federates six models, with corrosion run on its primary model and seismic clearance on all six.

**Table 3\. Corrosion results by test project.**

| Project | Model | Piping elements | Banded findings (C/H/M/L) | Data-quality notes |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| P46 | Clinic\_HVAC (IFC2x3) | 77 | 0 | 346 |
| P47 | WRH fire (IFC4) | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| P48 | Duplex\_Plumbing (IFC2x3) | 478 | 155 (147/0/8/0) | 1,822 |
| P49 | wbdg\_office\_mep (IFC2x3) | 2,748 | 319 (73/0/246/0) | 10,518 |
| P50 | WRH sprinkler (IFC4) | 12,136 | 11,051 (0/0/11,049/2) | 37,499 |
| P51 | 6 models, primary WRH plumbing (IFC4) | primary only | 0 | 29,181 |
| Total |   |   | 11,525 (220/0/11,303/2) | 79,366 |

 

![][image1]

Figure 1\. Band share of banded corrosion findings per project (P46, P47 and P51 returned none).

**Interpretation.** Of 11,525 banded findings, 11,303 (98.1%) are Medium, 220 are Critical, 2 are Low and none are High (Figure 1); the engines also raised 79,366 data-quality notes. This distribution does not show that the band thresholds are miscalibrated; it reflects the information the models contain. None of the models records operating temperature or service environment on its pipework, and few elements are assigned materials. GC-001, CC-001 and XM-001 therefore returned data-quality notes rather than guessing. Only MC-001 and MM-001 returned verdicts, and they scored the same defaulted inputs on almost every element, giving fixed scores: MC-001 0.756 (Critical) or 0.396 (Medium) and MM-001 0.40 (Medium). The pooled share is also dominated by one model: P50 alone contributes 11,049 Medium findings, while P48 is 95% Critical. The band distribution therefore measures model data completeness as much as corrosion risk.

**Seismic clearance.** SB-001 on the federated P51 (six models) raised 11,185 findings (115 Critical, 1,599 High, 9,471 Medium), in about six minutes.

**Verification.** Every CC-001 score on a 378-finding demonstration model was recomputed by hand from the published formula and matched the engine exactly (maximum deviation 0.000). Agreement with expert judgement was measured with the Validation Matrix (Appendix): 38 findings (P48: 18, P49: 20; seed 1, up to 10 per band) were labelled blind. The labels were AI-proposed from each element's system and finding evidence, then reviewed and confirmed by the expert. Exact agreement was 10.5% (4 of 38\) and Cohen's κ was −0.04, no better than chance (Figure 2). All 20 tool Critical findings were downgraded (to Medium 7, Low 9, No risk 4), so at the ≥High action threshold every one was a false positive. At ≥Medium the tool missed no expert-positive finding (recall 1.0, 11 of 11\) but raised 27 false alarms (precision 0.29). On defaulted inputs the tool is therefore conservative: it misses no risk, but cannot separate a dwelling's cold-water main from an office's low-use hot-water branch, a building-type judgement the expert made and the models do not encode. Client IFC samples with real temperature and material data have been approved to repeat this comparison.

Figure 2\. Tool result against expert evaluation, pooled over P48 and P49 (MC-001 findings; labels AI-proposed, expert-confirmed).

## **6.0 Limitations, Ethical Considerations and Risk Analysis** 

### **6.1 Limitations**

(1) Baseline validation combines synthetic architectural test pairs (ARCH golden/broken) and public multi-storey federated IFC models; extending automated testing to proprietary mega-project BIM datasets requires client data-sharing agreements. (2) Rule extraction is formally validated on dimensional and spatial egress/accessibility clauses (e.g. OBC 2012/2024 Division B Part 3, IBC 2021 Chapter 10, ADA 2010 Chapter 4); expanding automated coverage to complex structural and MEP calculation provisions remains ongoing work. (3) Bounding volumetric clearances and topological spatial containment checks are fully implemented in compute kernels, whereas dense as-built LiDAR point-cloud scan-vs-BIM registration remains on the future research roadmap. (4) Cost and schedule risk projections rely on standard international baseline indices and published unit rates unless a custom project-specific rate schedule is uploaded. (5) The LLM extraction pipeline is non-deterministic and involves API inference costs; it operates strictly as an asynchronous candidate proposal generator with structured Pydantic schema validation and mandatory human-in-the-loop expert review before rules are activated in production.

### **6.2 Ethical Considerations** 

BIMGuard is deliberately white-box and human-in-the-loop: the LLM never makes a compliance or risk decision, it only translates standards into candidate rules that a named human reviewer must approve before they act on any model. This matters because the domain is safety-critical; over-trusting an opaque model could pass a non-compliant design. Every rule is traceable to its source clause and standard, and every human approval is logged, an audit trail aligned with ISO 19650 information management and, for UK higher-risk buildings, the Building Safety Act "golden thread". Further considerations: respecting standards/IP licensing for the codes ingested; guarding against mis-interpretation bias when a clause is ambiguous (handled by flagging, not guessing); and being explicit that the tool augments, not replaces, the responsible engineer.

### **6.3 Risk Register** 

| \# | Risk | Likelihood/Impact | Mitigation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| R1 | Messy/incomplete IFC input | High / Med | ifc\_quality validate-repair-flag before checking |
| R2 | LLM hallucination / wrong rule | Med / High | needs\_review \+ source ref \+ mandatory human approval |
| R3 | Schedule slip before deadline | Med / High | Sprint plan \+ 2–3-day buffers; PM daily tracking |
| R4 | Distributed-team coordination / member availability | Med / Med | GitHub workflow; PM follow-up; modular ownership |
| R5 | Over-engineering vs core deliverable | Low / Med | Mentor guidance ("green" status); prioritise core solution \+ report |
| R6 | Vendor lock-in | Low / High | openBIM (IFC-in/BCF-out); no proprietary dependency |

## **7.0 Contributions to AECO Practice and Future Research Directions**

**Contributions**

BIMGuard AI contributes, to our knowledge, the first unified openBIM compliance intelligence platform that combines (a) AI-assisted, human-verified regulatory rule extraction from building code specifications, (b) deterministic rule-driven architectural and spatial compliance auditing, and (c) an interactive, empirical Tool-versus-Expert Validation Matrix emitting vendor-neutral BCF 2.1 deliverables. 

Four primary contributions advance AECO practice and automated compliance research:
1. **Closing the Compliance Latency Gap**: By shifting code compliance checking from late-stage manual review to continuous automated design-stage validation, non-compliant geometries are flagged when redesign costs are an order of magnitude lower.
2. **Responsible Human-in-the-Loop AI Architecture**: Rather than treating generative models as black-box compliance arbiters, BIMGuard demonstrates a white-box architecture where LLMs serve strictly as regulatory translators proposing structured candidate rules into a database-audited schema. Every rule requires explicit domain expert sign-off, fulfilling the "golden thread" traceability mandates of ISO 19650 and the UK Building Safety Act.
3. **Rigorous Empirical Validation & Inter-Annotator Agreement**: We establish an open-source evaluation benchmark with a human-annotated OBC 9.8 gold set and confusion-matrix scoring of live extraction (inter-annotator agreement and cross-jurisdiction transfer are not yet measured). The platform incorporates an in-app stratified Validation Matrix providing live confusion matrices, Wilson score 95% confidence intervals, and bootstrap Cohen's $\kappa$ metrics against blind expert ground truth.
4. **Interoperable, Vendor-Neutral Delivery**: By consuming openBIM IFC models and producing standardized BCF 2.1 issue reports linked with cost and schedule risk implications, the platform bridges technical engineering audits directly into project management coordination workflows without proprietary CAD/BIM vendor lock-in.

**Future research directions**

(1) Expand the golden regulatory rule catalog across structural, mechanical, and fire-safety engineering chapters, testing multi-domain semantic transfer. 
(2) Deploy active learning and reinforcement from human feedback (RLHF) so expert corrections in the drafting UI iteratively fine-tune few-shot extraction prompts. 
(3) Integrate 3D spatial scene graphs and topological graph neural networks (GNNs) for holistic circulation and egress route network optimization. 
(4) Implement dense LiDAR point-cloud scan-to-BIM geometric registration to extend compliance checking from design models to as-built construction stages. 
(5) Extend the decoupled API architecture with autonomous multi-agent assistants that synthesize multi-discipline compliance summaries for executive stakeholder reporting.

## **Proposal for discussion: tool-versus-expert Validation Matrix**

Added by Shane, 25 September 2026, for the team to consider. It is not part of the report or its word count. It describes a feature built into BIMGuard on 24 September 2026 that may help answer the mentor's request to show where the tool is right and where it is wrong.

**Why it exists.** BIMGuard is rule-based, so its findings have no automatic ground truth. The accepted alternative is sample-based validation: an expert independently classifies a sample of the tool's findings, and the two classifications are compared in a confusion matrix.

**How it works (Figure A1).** 1\) For a project and audit type (corrosion or seismic), the tool takes its assessed findings; data-quality notes are excluded because they report missing inputs, not a risk judgement. 2\) It draws a stratified sample of up to N findings per band (default 10), round-robin across rules so one prolific rule cannot crowd out the others, with a fixed seed so the sample in a report can be reproduced. Stratifying matters: a run can hold 11,000 Medium findings and 5 High ones, and a uniform sample would contain no High findings at all. 3\) The expert reviews each sampled finding blind (the tool's band is hidden by default) and labels it Critical, High, Medium, Low or No risk, where No risk marks a false alarm. Labels are stored in the database with the tool's band at the time, so a later re-run cannot rewrite the history. A label can also be given from any Finding Report ("Expert evaluation"). 4\) Labels pooled over any selected projects form a matrix of tool band (rows) against expert band (columns), with exact agreement, Cohen's κ and per-band precision and recall. κ is reported because a tool that put everything in one band could score high raw agreement and still show κ \= 0\. 5\) The matrix is collapsed at an "action required" threshold (≥High or ≥Medium) into TP, FP, FN and TN, with accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1; a ratio with an empty denominator shows as "–", not 0\. 6\) Each matrix exports as SVG, PNG or CSV.

**Where to find it.** Project sidebar → Compliance → Validation Matrix, and the "Expert evaluation" control in each Finding Report.

**Status.** 38 labels are recorded (P48: 18, P49: 20). Results are reported in 5.2 (Figure 2): exact agreement 10.5%, Cohen's κ −0.04, recall 1.0 and precision 0.29 at ≥Medium. The labels were AI-proposed and confirmed by the expert, and this should be disclosed wherever they are reported. Figures A2–A4 were captured before labelling (n \= 1).

**For discussion.** The same pattern could validate the other pillars: the architectural audit (an expert labels pass or fail on the golden and broken reference models) and rule extraction (field-level correct or incorrect, the confusion matrix planned for 5.1). One consistent evaluation method across the report would be a strength. The team decides whether to adopt it.
